questions.stem: Read Passage B: "When did we decide that a bored child was a failure of parenting? Last weekend I watched a boy of about seven sit on a bench, swinging his legs, doing precisely nothing for twenty minutes. His father apologised to me. 'He's bored,' he said, the way you might say 'he's bleeding.' He then handed the boy a tablet, and the bench went quiet. We have built an entire economy on the promise that no child should ever have to be bored. It is a promise we should refuse to keep. Boredom is not a gap in a child's education; it is the workshop. A mind with nothing to do starts, reluctantly, to make things: games with pebbles, worlds out of cloud shapes, the first sentences of stories nobody asked for. Researchers at the University of Central Lancashire found that children made to wait through dull tasks afterwards outscored their entertained peers on creative tests. The bored brain does not switch off; it forages. The boy on the bench will be fine either way. But when we rush to fill every empty minute, we are not rescuing our children from boredom. We are evicting them from the room where their imagination does its best work." State the writer's main claim, and give ONE reason the writer offers for it.
markscheme: B1: the main claim — we should stop rushing to entertain children / boredom is good for children ('a promise we should refuse to keep')
B2: one offered reason — boredom sets the mind making things, or bored children outscored entertained peers on creative tests
questions.modelAnswer: The claim is that we should stop treating boredom as a problem to be fixed — 'a promise we should refuse to keep'. One reason offered: a mind with nothing to do starts to make things, supported by the research finding that bored children outscored their entertained peers on creative tests.

questions.stem: Look again at Passage B (Question 1). The father speaks of boredom 'the way you might say 'he's bleeding''. Name the technique in this comparison and state its effect.
markscheme: B1: the technique — a simile (an exaggerated comparison)
B2: the effect — it ridicules the parent's panic, presenting the reaction to boredom as absurdly overblown
questions.modelAnswer: It is a simile — the father says 'he's bored' the way you might say 'he's bleeding'. The exaggeration mocks the panic: boredom is treated like a medical emergency, which makes the parent's reaction look absurd and primes the reader to side with the writer.

questions.stem: Look again at Passage B (Question 1). For the claim 'Boredom is not a gap in a child's education; it is the workshop' to hold, what must the writer be assuming?
markscheme: B1: the assumption — children left unentertained will generate their own play and ideas, rather than simply switching off
B2: why it is needed — if bored children produced nothing, boredom could not be called 'the workshop' and the claim collapses
questions.modelAnswer: The writer assumes that a bored child will eventually start inventing — games, worlds, stories — rather than disengaging entirely. The claim needs that assumption: only if boredom reliably triggers creation can it be called 'the workshop' instead of a gap.

questions.stem: Look again at Passage B (Question 1). The writer supports the claim with the bench anecdote and with the University of Central Lancashire research. Which is the stronger evidence, and why?
markscheme: B1: the judgement — the research is the stronger evidence
B2: the reason — it is systematic and measured (groups compared on tests), not a single observed moment
B3: a credited caveat — the anecdote illustrates but cannot prove, or the research is cited without figures to inspect
questions.modelAnswer: The research is stronger: it compares groups of children on creative tests, so it measures the very effect the writer claims. The bench anecdote is one observed moment — it illustrates the attitude under attack but proves nothing. Credit either caveat: the anecdote cannot be generalised, or the research is cited with no figures to examine.

questions.stem: Write ONE paragraph (three to five sentences) challenging the view in Passage B (Question 1) and arguing that children benefit from structured entertainment. Use your own words — do not lift phrases from the passage.
markscheme: B1: a clear challenging position is taken and held throughout the paragraph
B2: the challenge is developed with reasoning (a because/therefore move), not merely asserted
B3: controlled argumentative register in the student's own words — no phrases lifted from the passage
questions.modelAnswer: Sample: Structured entertainment is not the enemy of imagination; often it is the fuel. A well-made film or game hands a child new worlds to raid for their own play, which an empty afternoon cannot guarantee. Nor does every idle child invent — some simply fret. A healthy week needs both boredom and structure, not a ban on one of them.

questions.stem: Look again at Passage B (Question 1). Identify ONE counter-argument the writer does not address, and explain how it weakens the conclusion.
markscheme: B1: a valid missing counter-argument — e.g. some children respond to boredom with anxiety, not invention / much screen entertainment is itself creative / parents cannot always supervise unstructured time
B2: the mechanism — how that point undercuts the promise that 'no child should ever have to be bored'
B3: the link is tied to a specific claim or phrase in the passage
questions.modelAnswer: One missing counter-argument: not every bored child forages — some become anxious or disruptive without structure. That undercuts the absolute claim that 'no child should ever have to be bored', because for those children entertainment is a need rather than a rescue from growth; the conclusion survives only in a weaker, some-of-the-time form.

questions.stem: A descriptive composition opens with the title 'The Empty Playground'. Write the opening three or four sentences. The marks reward description, not plot.
markscheme: B1: a strong, immediate sense of place and atmosphere
B2: controlled, purposeful imagery — details chosen for effect, not adjective-piling
B3: remains descriptive — no character arrives and launches a story (narrative drift)
questions.modelAnswer: Sample: The chains of the swings ticked against their posts in the wind. Chalk drawings had faded to pale ghosts on the tarmac, half washed away by a week of rain. A single glove lay curled on the roundabout like something small that had given up. Beyond the railings, the estate went on with its evening, lit windows ignoring the empty park.

questions.stem: Write a one-sentence opening hook for a narrative called 'The Letter', then name the hook technique you have used.
markscheme: B1: the opening creates immediate tension or questions — the reader wants the second line
B2: the technique is correctly named — e.g. in medias res / withheld information / foreshadowing / an incongruous detail
questions.modelAnswer: Sample: 'The envelope had no stamp, no address and no right to be on my doorstep at six in the morning — but it had my name, in my dead sister's handwriting.' Technique: withheld information with an incongruous detail — the reader is handed questions before answers.
